presentingComplaint: Non-healing sole ulcer with a foul discharge noticed on a sock, but no pain and no fever.
history: Type 2 diabetic for 22 years with established peripheral sensory neuropathy and prior right first-toe amputation. He denies pain entirely because of dense neuropathy, and only sought review because his daughter noticed malodorous staining and swelling of the mid-foot. There has been no rigor, no documented fever at home, and appetite is unchanged. Glycaemic control has been poor (self-monitored fasting values 200-260 mg/dL). He has intermittent claudication and absent pedal pulses on the affected side. No recent hospitalisation or antibiotics. The subtlety of the presentation - an afebrile, pain-free patient with a deceptively 'quiet' foot - masks deep infection.
examination: A 3 cm plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head with surrounding erythema and warmth extending to the mid-foot; the wound is malodorous with purulent drainage. Sterile blunt probe reaches bone (positive probe-to-bone). Callus overlies the ulcer margin. Absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses with delayed capillary refill; monofilament sensation lost to the ankle. No crepitus, no haemorrhagic bullae, and no pain out of proportion. Systemically the patient looks well and is not toxic.
imaging: Plain radiograph of the foot: cortical erosion and periosteal reaction at the first metatarsal head with adjacent soft-tissue swelling, consistent with osteomyelitis. Ankle-brachial index 0.6 indicating peripheral arterial disease. MRI (if obtained) would confirm marrow oedema/osteomyelitis.
microbiology: Deep wound/curettage culture (not superficial swab) sent; Gram stain shows mixed gram-positive cocci and gram-negative bacilli. Bone biopsy recommended for definitive osteomyelitis pathogen and susceptibility. Blood cultures sent given systemic inflammatory markers.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute gout / crystal arthritis of the midfoot
finalDiagnosis: Moderate-to-severe diabetic foot infection with underlying osteomyelitis and peripheral arterial disease, presenting atypically without pain or fever due to sensory neuropathy.
citations: IWGDF/IDSA - Diagnosis and Management of Diabetic Foot Infections - 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Diabetic Foot / Osteomyelitis
stewardship: Moderate-to-severe diabetic foot infection with osteomyelitis. Obtain deep tissue/bone specimens before or at initiation of therapy. Empiric cover should include streptococci, staphylococci (with MRSA cover given chronicity and prior amputation), aerobic gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, then de-escalate to culture-directed therapy. Urgent vascular assessment for revascularisation and surgical debridement; antibiotics alone are insufficient with bone involvement and PAD.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic combinations without monitoring given creatinine 1.4 mg/dL; dose-adjust vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam to renal function.
Do not rely on superficial swab cultures to guide therapy.
edgeCases: Absence of pain and fever does NOT exclude serious deep infection in a neuropathic diabetic - a classic atypical trap.
Positive probe-to-bone with elevated ESR strongly predicts osteomyelitis.
Coexisting peripheral arterial disease worsens prognosis and mandates vascular input.
expectedMaiK: Recognise diabetic foot infection with osteomyelitis despite an atypically painless, afebrile presentation; secure deep cultures, image for bone involvement, assess perfusion, and start guideline-concordant broad empiric antibiotics alongside surgical/vascular referral.
expectedNextQuestions: Duration of the ulcer and any prior foot infections or amputations?
Any recent antibiotics or hospitalisation (MDR/MRSA risk)?
Claudication or rest pain suggesting arterial insufficiency?
